chapter: Ben Webster and Jim and Andy's
title: Three musicians' bars: Hurley's, Jim and Andy's, Charlie's
summary: Maxwell explains the New York musicians' bars and why NBC players moved from Hurley's to Jim and Andy's.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Absolutely. Well, Ben was something like that, friendship meant so much to him, as you say. You know, I wish you would talk a little about -- this concerns your life and you were certainly one of the customers of Jim and

Andy's. I think for posterity people should know about them. In some of the several interviews I've had with people, I don't remember asking any body this but you, Jimmy, and sort of explain Jim and Andy's. Just, this was a bar, and who Jim was and who Andy was, do you remember?

Well, it was like an institution. Originally there were three musicians' bars in New York. There was Hurley's Bar, that was in the NBC Building, that was where all the NBC musicians went. And the announcers. There was Jim and Andy's over a block away, and that's where the ABC musicians went, although they worked in the same building at that time, only ABC musicians went there. And then there was that place over on 7th, Charlie's, where the --
Yeah, you know, the club date and road bands.
-- or upper classes, according to which group you belonged to.

Yeah. Now, Hurley's was a real stinking place, clip joint. They never bought a drink, they would cheat you out of the money, and they were mean bastards there. Finally they just drove everybody out. So all the musicians from

NBC went over to Jim and Andy's. Then little by little the word got around, this is where the working men hang out, so all the musicians started hanging out, thinking they could hustle a gig, meet the big boys or something, I don't know. And that place used to be jammed.
